background: In April 2024, 15M records from the online florist Blooms Today were listed for sale on a popular hacking forum . The most recent data in the breach corpus was from November 2023 and appeared alongside 3.2M unique email addresses, names, phone numbers physical addresses and partial credit card data (card type, 4 digits of the number and expiry date). The breach did not expose sufficient card data to make purchases.
Blooms Today did not respond when contacted about the incident.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
motive: In April 2024, 15M records from the online florist Blooms Today were listed for sale on a popular hacking forum .
outcome: 3,184,010 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Names, Partial credit card data, Phone numbers, Physical addresses.
editorial: A florist's database has a property most retail data does not: a large share of the people in it never bought anything. Gift orders carry a recipient, a name, an address, often a phone number, belonging to somebody who has no account, agreed to no terms, and will never receive a notification because the company has no relationship with them to notify.

Whether this particular corpus separates buyers from recipients is not something the breach record can tell you, and it is worth being precise about that rather than assuming the worst. What the record does say is that 3.2 million addresses appeared alongside names, phone numbers, physical addresses and partial card data, in a file offered for sale roughly five months after the most recent data in it was created.

Nobody was watching in between. The exposure that follows is a delivery scam, and flowers make it unusually effective. An unexpected delivery is plausible for almost anyone, confirming an address for one feels harmless, and a message that already has your address and the last four digits of a card reads as legitimate.
A courier that cannot deliver does not need your card details to try again, and a florist does not ask for them by text.

fields.name: Physical addresses
fields.why: Where someone actually lives. Combined with a name this moves the risk off the internet.

fields.name: Phone numbers
fields.why: Enables SIM-swap attacks against SMS two-factor codes, and puts the number on scam-call lists indefinitely.

fields.name: Partial credit card data
fields.why: Not enough to spend, but enough to convince a victim that a caller is genuinely from their bank.

fields.name: Names
fields.why: Turns an anonymous address into an identified person, which is what makes targeted phishing possible.

fields.name: Email addresses
fields.why: The address becomes a confirmed, active target, expect more phishing, better aimed.

actions: Move two-factor authentication off SMS and onto an authenticator app, which a SIM swap cannot intercept.
Be sceptical of post and callers who already know your address, knowing it is no longer evidence of anything.
Expect better-aimed phishing. A message that already knows your name and where you have an account is the whole point of a breach like this.
breach.scale_line: That is about 12% of the population of Australia.
